summary.text: The base rate fallacy is the mistake of ignoring how common something is overall in favour of details about one specific case.
A test that seems highly accurate can still flag more innocent people than real cases when the thing it looks for is rare in the group tested.
In a breathalyzer example, one driver in a thousand is drunk and sober drivers test drunk 5% of the time, so a positive driver is drunk only about 2% of the time, not 95%.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Prosecutor's fallacy or defense attorney's fallacy, in law proceedings

facts.label: False positive paradox
facts.value: More false positive results than true positives

facts.label: Breathalyzer case
facts.value: A positive reading means about a 2% chance of drunkenness

facts.label: Same test, two groups
facts.value: A positive is over 93% reliable in one group, 29% in another

facts.label: Alarm system
facts.value: Despite a 99% hit rate, a ring means a terrorist only near 1%

items.prompt: A rare allergy affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test wrongly flags 5% of people who lack it and never misses real cases. At a random screening, you test positive. Roughly how likely is it that you have the allergy?

options.label: About 95%, because the test is almost always right
About 50%, because you either have it or you do not
About 5%, because that is the test's false alarm rate
About 2%, because false alarms far outnumber real cases

items.explain: Among 1,000 people, 1 real case is flagged along with about 50 false alarms, so only about 1 in 51 positives is real.

items.prompt: A camera flags wanted criminals 99% accurately, but it scans 10,000 people a day and almost none are wanted. Why is its list of flagged people likely to be mostly innocent?

options.label: A small error rate applied to a huge innocent crowd gives more mistakes than real hits
The camera is secretly less accurate on innocent people than it claims
Wanted people usually avoid cameras, so they rarely show up on the list
Large crowds always make the camera's results random

items.explain: Even a small fraction of the much larger innocent group produces more positives than a large fraction of the tiny wanted group.

items.prompt: A tester who has only worked with a group where infection is common starts using the same test on a group where it is rare. What should the tester expect about positive results?

options.label: They stay equally reliable, since the test is the same
They become more reliable, since the rare group has fewer cases
They are less reliable, since who is tested matters as well as accuracy
They no longer carry any information, since the groups differ

items.explain: The chance that a positive is real depends on the characteristics of the group tested, so a result that usually meant infection can mostly be false positives in a low-prevalence group.

items.prompt: A town's alarm rings 99% of the time when it scans a wanted person. Someone says: it rang, so there is a 99% chance this person is wanted. What is the error?

options.label: The alarm cannot be trusted at all when it rings
The chance of ringing for a wanted person was confused with the chance of being wanted after a ring
The 99% should be changed to 100%, since the alarm rarely misses
Rings that sound in a crowd should be counted twice

items.explain: The chance that the bell rings given a terrorist and the chance of a terrorist given the bell are different, unrelated quantities. In the example the second is near 1%, not near 99%.

items.prompt: The 2% drunk-driver figure assumes the driver was stopped truly at random. Suppose the driver was stopped for weaving. What changes?

options.label: Nothing, since the breathalyzer reading alone decides the answer
The answer becomes exactly 95%, since the reading is a positive
The calculation must also weigh how likely drunk and sober drivers are to weave
The answer drops to zero, since the stop was not random

items.explain: The result depends on the stop being random. With another reason for stopping, the calculation also involves how likely drunk and non-drunk drivers are to drive badly.

items.prompt: An identical alarm is installed in a second city that has no wanted people at all. It still rings for 1 in 100 innocent people. When it rings there, what is the chance the person is wanted?

options.label: 1%, matching the alarm's false positive rate
99%, matching the alarm's accuracy
Zero, since there is no one wanted to detect
50%, since the alarm is as likely wrong as right

items.explain: Every ring in that city is for an innocent person, so the chance of a wanted person given a ring is 0%.
